title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
formal: For every fixed alphabet size \(a\ge2\), is deterministic minimization of complete finite automata over \([a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) possible in \(O(n)\) worst-case time on the word-RAM defined below? More explicitly, the target is \[\forall a\ge2\ \exists M_a,C_a,n_a\ \forall n\ge n_a\ \forall A\text{ with }n\text{ states},\quad M_a(A)\text{ outputs a smallest equivalent complete DFA in at most }C_a n\text{ steps}.\] Here \(M_a\) is a single finite program independent of \(n\); \(C_a\) and \(n_a\) may depend on \(a\), and \(n_a\ge a\) may be assumed. The task is exact language-preserving minimization, with no prescribed canonical naming of output states.
definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an input DFA is \(A=([n],[a],\delta,s,F)\), where \(\delta:[n]\times[a]\to[n]\) is total, \(s\in[n]\), and \(F\subseteq[n]\). Its explicit input consists of \(n\), \(s\), the \(an\) transition targets, and \(n\) accepting-state bits, one target or bit per input word. Extend \(\delta\) to finite words by \(\delta^*(q,\varepsilon)=q\) and \(\delta^*(q,ub)=\delta(\delta^*(q,u),b)\). The recognized language is \(\{u:\delta^*(s,u)\in F\}\). The output is an explicit complete DFA \(B=([k],[a],\delta',s',F')\), \(1\le k\le n\), recognizing exactly that language, with \(k\) minimal among all complete DFAs over the same alphabet. Unreachable input states may be discarded; no equivalence partition for them is required. Both input and output transitions are explicitly represented.

Use one sequential deterministic word-RAM with word length \(w=\lceil2\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), addressed word memory and finitely many registers. Reading or writing one addressed word, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), Boolean bit operations, shifts by an amount less than \(w\), comparisons and conditional branches each cost one step. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, oracle instruction or externally supplied lookup table is available. The finite program may depend on the fixed alphabet size but not on the input size. All algorithmic preprocessing, auxiliary-table construction, initialization and output writing are charged to the running time; memory beyond the input has a fixed blank initial value. The asymptotic target is considered for \(n\ge n_a\ge a\), so the explicit \(an\)-word transition table fits the chosen word address space. Finitely many smaller sizes for each fixed alphabet are finite exceptions to the asymptotic claim. This spells out the input-addressing convention without changing the saved logarithmic word formula. The cost is in word operations, not bit operations: the input uses \(\Theta(n)\) words for fixed \(a\). There is no randomization, expected-time qualification, distribution on inputs, language approximation or promise on the transition graph.

context_blocks.text: Two reachable states are equivalent exactly when every continuation word is either accepted from both or rejected from both. A smallest recognizer retains one representative of each such behavior. The task asks for the resulting explicit automaton, not merely a test of whether the input is already minimal.

Hopcroft’s algorithm minimizes a complete DFA in \(O(an\log n)\) time. For a fixed alphabet this is \(O(n\log n)\), while the input and a largest possible minimal output each occupy only linearly many words. The target is therefore removal of one logarithmic factor in worst-case sequential time.

Partition refinement begins with blocks distinguished by acceptance and repeatedly separates states whose transitions lead to different blocks. The 2023 lower-bound paper formalizes costs of such refinements and proves a logarithmic-factor obstruction even on deterministic systems with two actions. Its theorem quantifies over that method class, not over all multiplication-capable word-RAM programs.

Unary automata have a functional-graph structure that admits linear-time methods outside ordinary partition refinement. The saved target deliberately starts at alphabet size two, where two successor functions can interact. The successful unary case cannot be substituted for the multi-letter statement.

There are also linear-time results for special transition graphs, such as those whose nontrivial strongly connected components are cycles. These are meaningful positive cases but do not impose the arbitrary transition-graph guarantee requested here.

The source concerns symbolic automata, where transitions can carry predicates describing large or infinite alphabets. This card uses only its ordinary finite-alphabet minimization baseline. The precise word operations, input layout and uniformity convention are editorial choices already present in the saved target; they are not attributed as a conjecture made verbatim by the source authors.

why: DFA minimization is a basic preprocessing step for recognizers, regular-language operations and finite-state verification. Its classical algorithm is almost linear, and the logarithmic factor has resisted removal for general transition graphs. Resolving the target would distinguish an inherent cost of the problem from the cost of the partition-refinement paradigm.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation, including correctness, minimality, explicit output and the stated RAM cost. A positive proof must cover every fixed \(a\ge2\) by a uniform-in-\(n\) finite program and fixed constants. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(a\ge2\), every correct program in this full RAM model fails an \(O(n)\) worst-case bound: no constants \(C,n_0\) work for all sufficiently large inputs. A lower bound restricted to partition refinement, a comparison model or one particular minimization algorithm does not prove this negation. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional version.

progress.text: The classical Hopcroft bound, recorded in the source, gives O(an log n) worst-case minimization time.
Almeida and Zeitoun establish linear minimization for automata whose nontrivial strongly connected components are cycles.
The cited symbolic-automata paper identifies Hopcroft’s algorithm as the ordinary-DFA baseline and distinguishes its cost from symbolic-alphabet costs.
The checked lower-bound paper proves barriers for sequential partition-refinement algorithms, including deterministic two-action instances, without an unrestricted RAM lower bound.
The fixed alphabet, explicit word-RAM model and stronger unrestricted target were checked; bounded later-primary searches found no matching linear algorithm or full-model impossibility result.

status_note: The source supports the classical O(an log n) baseline, not the exact editorial word-RAM statement as a verbatim open question. The 2023 primary lower-bound paper explicitly restricts its result to partition-refinement algorithms. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching unrestricted deterministic linear-time algorithm or lower bound in the saved RAM model. This is a source-supported editorial target with a dated status check, not a proof of present openness.

source_formulation.text: Can the classical O(n log n) worst-case bound for minimization over a fixed finite alphabet be improved to linear time by an unrestricted sequential algorithm?

sentences: A deterministic finite automaton can be minimized by merging reachable states that accept exactly the same continuation words.
The question asks whether every complete automaton over any fixed alphabet of at least two letters can be minimized in deterministic linear worst-case word-RAM time.
The output must be an explicit smallest automaton recognizing exactly the original language, and all preprocessing and output work count.
Classical algorithms take O(n log n) time, while known logarithmic-factor lower bounds concern partition refinement rather than every algorithm in the stated model.
A resolution would determine whether the extra logarithmic cost reflects the general problem or the structure of its classical algorithms.
